description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

book.title: Factfulness
book.author: Hans Rosling, Ola Rosling, and Anna Rosling Rönnlund

cards.title: The World Is Better Than You Think
cards.subtitle: You asked Nobel laureates basic questions about global health. They scored worse than random guessing.
body: Child mortality rate: halved in 20 years. Extreme poverty: from 50% to under 10% in two generations.
Every educated audience Rosling tested got these facts backward.
cards.takeaway: Your worldview is decades out of date.

cards.title: The Gap Instinct Divides the World Wrong
cards.subtitle: Your mental map has two boxes: rich countries and poor countries. Five billion people don't fit in either.
body: Most humans live on income levels 2 and 3. They have electricity, send kids to school, and own a bike.
'Developing world' lumps Bangladesh with Burundi.
cards.takeaway: The middle you keep ignoring is where most people are.

cards.title: Most People Live in the Middle
cards.subtitle: Level 1: barefoot, no electricity. Level 4: car, passport, college. Your mental model has those two.
body: Level 2: a bike, a bucket, electricity sometimes. Level 3: a motorbike, a washing machine, kids in school.

• Majority of children are vaccinated
• Majority of girls go to school
cards.takeaway: The four-level framework reveals what binary thinking hides.

cards.title: Straight Lines Are Rare in Reality
cards.subtitle: Population has been rising for 200 years. You drew a straight line up. The line already bent.
body: Birth rates are falling everywhere. The curve that looked exponential is flattening into an S.
You're still preparing for the apocalypse from a trend that ended a decade ago.
cards.takeaway: The straight line assumption breaks every forecast.

cards.title: Fear Distorts Risk Assessment
cards.subtitle: You're afraid of sharks. Heart disease will kill you. Plane crashes scare you. Car rides kill 1.3 million people a year.
body: The vivid image wins. Shark attack: front page. Air pollution deaths: page seventeen.
Your brain is wired to fear spectacle, not statistics.
cards.takeaway: Policy follows fear, not mortality tables.

cards.title: Size Without Context Is Meaningless
cards.subtitle: Four million babies died this year. You're horrified. Forty years ago the number was fourteen million.
body: The single number is designed to shock. The comparison shows one of the greatest achievements in human history.

• Compared to what?
• Per capita or absolute?
cards.takeaway: The number alone is a weapon, not information.

cards.title: Generalization Erases the Useful Details
cards.subtitle: You said 'Africa' like it's one place. It's 54 countries. Tunisia and Mozambique have nothing in common.
body: Morocco's literacy rate is 75%. Niger's is 30%. Both are 'Africa' in your mental model.
Within-group variation exceeds between-group variation.
cards.takeaway: Disaggregate or stay wrong.

cards.title: Destiny Is a Story, Not a Fact
cards.subtitle: Bangladesh was the case study for hopeless poverty in the 1970s. Its child survival rate now beats the US in some states.
body: South Korea went from Level 1 to Level 4 in one generation. Iran's birth rate dropped faster than Sweden's.
The countries you wrote off changed while you were busy explaining why they couldn't.
cards.takeaway: Destiny is yesterday's data treated as prophecy.

cards.title: Single Perspectives Miss the System
cards.subtitle: The doctor sees disease. The economist sees markets. The activist sees injustice. Same problem, three explanations.
body: Give an expert a complex problem and they'll explain it using their one framework.
Poverty isn't just economics. Health isn't just medicine. You need multiple lenses.
cards.takeaway: The useful perspective is the one you forgot to ask.

cards.title: Blame Blocks Understanding
cards.subtitle: You found the villain in twenty minutes. The system that produced the outcome took decades to build.
body: Blame feels decisive. Point at the company, the politician, the group. Punishment follows. The problem continues.
Systemic outcomes don't need villains—they need feedback loops.
cards.takeaway: Blame is energy aimed at revenge, not prevention.

cards.title: Urgency Creates Bad Decisions
cards.subtitle: The headline says act NOW. You skip the analysis. The intervention makes it worse.
body: Ebola: panic built bad quarantines, wasted resources, and spread the disease faster.

• You feel decisive but you're just reactive
• Most deadlines are manufactured
cards.takeaway: Take a breath. Check the data. Then move.

cards.title: Negativity Gets More Attention Than Progress
cards.subtitle: One factory explodes: front page. A thousand factories run safely all year: silence.
body: Smallpox got eradicated over decades. No headline captured it. Plane crashes sell papers.
Your information diet is systematically skewed toward catastrophe.
cards.takeaway: Good news requires active searching because it won't find you.

cards.title: Data Without Questions Is Just Noise
cards.subtitle: You looked at the number. Formed an opinion. Never asked what it was measuring.
body: Same dataset, opposite conclusions, depending on the question. 'Is it bad?' tells you nothing.
Data doesn't speak. You interrogate it or you just see what you want.
cards.takeaway: The question determines the answer.

cards.title: The Media Isn't Lying—It's Selecting
cards.subtitle: Plane crashes make the news. Safe landings don't. You think flying got more dangerous.
body: Journalists aren't lying. They're selecting abnormality. News is, by definition, the unusual.
Consume it without a data baseline and you get progressively more wrong.
cards.takeaway: Data literacy is the antidote to headline poisoning.

cards.title: Poverty Levels Tell You More Than Country Labels
cards.subtitle: A Level 2 family in Kenya has more in common with a Level 2 family in India than with their own country's elite.
body: Income level predicts daily life better than nationality. Same level, same challenges.
Level 3 in Nigeria looks like Level 3 in Peru.
cards.takeaway: Income bracket tells you more than passport.

cards.title: Slow Progress Is Still Progress
cards.subtitle: Girls' education went from 60% to 90% in thirty years. Reshapes civilizations. Never made a headline.
body: Change that takes a generation is invisible day to day. You see the chaos in the foreground.

• Gradual is invisible
• Invisible doesn't mean unimportant
cards.takeaway: Historians celebrate what journalists missed.

cards.title: Extreme Poverty Dropped and Nobody Noticed
cards.subtitle: Extreme poverty: 85% of humanity in 1800. Under 10% today. Population quadrupled during the same period.
body: No ribbon-cutting ceremony. A thousand small improvements compounded across two centuries.
Medicine, agriculture, trade, governance. And most people believe poverty is rising.
cards.takeaway: Not knowing this breaks every policy debate and donation decision.

cards.title: Educated People Get These Questions Wrong Too
cards.subtitle: Professors, Nobel laureates, world leaders—all tested. All scored worse than random guessing.
body: Not a problem of intelligence. Problem of outdated models. They learned their worldview in 1985.
Their confidence made them worse—certain about facts that changed.
cards.takeaway: Education doesn't protect you from stale maps.

cards.title: Categories Collapse When You Look Closely
cards.subtitle: Zoom in on 'Africa.' Find 54 countries. Zoom in on one country. Find urban and rural opposites.
body: Every generalization is lossy compression. 'The average' hides the spread.
Averages flatten what matters. Variation is the truth.
cards.takeaway: Disaggregate or stay blind.

cards.title: Factfulness Is a Practice, Not a Position
cards.subtitle: Your brain evolved for survival, not accuracy. Fear, blame, urgency—all useful on the savanna.
body: You can't delete your instincts. You can check them against evidence. Factfulness is that habit.
Biases don't disappear. Management beats denial.
cards.takeaway: It's seeing what's actually there.
